Page 1 of 3 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850 
 
RE: CMS-0062-P: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) 
Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
Facilitated Exchanges 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
Amazon.com, Inc. (Amazon) appreciates the opportunity to comment on efforts by the Centers for 
Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) on enabling more expeditious patient access to medications that 
individuals need.  
 
As a customer-obsessed company, we believe patients and providers benefit from healthcare that is 
convenient, accessible, and affordable. Efforts that advance a seamless, secure, and patient-centered 
digital health infrastructure will improve patients’ longitudinal engagement in their care journey, 
resulting in improved health outcomes and reduced healthcare expenditures. When combining secure 
data interoperability with new agentic AI solutions, technology can better empower individuals and 
remove friction that prevents access to care.  
 
For example, Amazon Pharmacy uses AI to get prescriptions into patients’ hands 90% faster by 
automatically structuring prescription data, predicting medication inventory needs, providing real-time 
price estimates without manual insurance entry, and enhancing customer support through AI-powered 
documentation analysis. One Medical is deploying generative AI to handle routine administrative tasks 
such as reviewing health records, routing messages, and automating workflows—giving providers more 
time to focus on patient care rather than paperwork. And, Amazon Connect Health—an agentic AI 
solution offered via Amazon Web Services (AWS)—can automate administrative tasks, such as prior 
authorization, to reduce the burden on both patients and providers.   
 
Broadly, Amazon supports provisions in the proposed rule that will leverage standards-based application 
programming interfaces (APIs) to facilitate data exchange among providers, payers, and pharmacies. 
Amazon has long supported and enabled interoperability, including as an early adopter in the 
administration’s Health Technology Ecosystem. Implementation and use of electronic standards for 
electronic prior authorization of medications will help patients and providers understand the eligibility 
requirements for certain drugs, and support more efficient adjudication of these requirements. 
Implementing these capabilities will address opaque cost and access requirements that, far too often, 
force patients to walk away empty-handed from the pharmacy counter. 
 
Page 2 of 3 
 
We appreciate CMS aligning electronic prior authorization for medical benefit drugs to the 2024 CMS 
Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule. That 2024 regulation requires impacted payers to 
leverage the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard for electronic prior 
authorization of services. Aligning electronic prior authorization for medical benefit drugs to the FHIR-
based approach taken for services will streamline implementation and more efficiently enable data 
exchange between healthcare providers and payers. AWS services can already support implementation 
of this FHIR-based approach. For example, AWS Healthlake leverages FHIR to enable healthcare 
organizations to securely share large volumes of health data in a queryable, standardized format at 
petabyte scale. AWS Healthlake already has capabilities—both for an individual record and bulk 
export—needed to enable FHIR-based electronic prior authorization and support adoption of the Da 
Vinci specifications mentioned in the 2024 final regulation and this proposed rule. 
 
However, we remain concerned that CMS intends to maintain use of National Council for Prescription 
Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards for electronic prior authorization for pharmacy benefit medications. 
Instead of dual-track standards that add complexity, aligning on a single approach to electronic prior 
authorization for all medical and pharmacy benefits will reduce burden and simplify adoption. 
 
CMS should establish a clear, consistent, end-to-end framework using FHIR-based APIs as the 
foundational standard for all prior authorization workflows across both medical and prescription 
benefits. This standardized model would enable simpler, more efficient experiences for patients, 
clinicians, pharmacies, and health plans to reduce reliance on manual, duplicative, or proprietary 
integrations. A single FHIR-based approach and interface can route the right data to the payer and 
support close to real-time adjudication—instead of necessitating complex mapping based on the 
medical or pharmacy benefits. In addition, adoption of NCPDP standards for drug electronic prior 
authorization will require backend translation between NCPDP and FHIR—both adding implementation 
costs and burden while maintaining the data exchange friction between systems that this proposed rule 
was designed to eliminate through a unified approach.  
 
CMS should assess whether to create an option for healthcare providers to use FHIR for electronic prior 
authorization of drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit. CMS should consider offering enforcement 
discretion—as needed—for organizations interested in leveraging FHIR for all electronic prior 
authorization transactions. If needed, CMS may also consider adopting NCPDP prior authorization 
standards for a limited number of years in parallel to FHIR, with a transition to FHIR-only electronic prior 
authorization within a few years.  
 
We are aware of efforts to establish an implementation guide for use of FHIR in pharmacy benefit 
electronic prior authorization transactions. We encourage CMS to adopt this FHIR-based approach, 
which is generating interest and collaboration across the standards community.  
 
In addition to the standards used for electronic prior authorization, we support CMS efforts to reduce 
response times—including the proposed requirement for qualified health plans to respond to prior 
authorization requests as expeditiously as needed for the individual’s health condition, and no later than 
72 hours from receiving the request. Electronic data exchange in conjunction with agentic AI tools can 
help providers and payers more seamlessly identify and respond to information requests, and 
streamline reviews to expedite patient access to medications for which they are eligible. 
 
Last, we also support CMS efforts to establish other building blocks needed to support more efficient 
interoperability—specifically requirements for payers to report API endpoint availability. This 
Page 3 of 3 
 
information, once aggregated, will enable the creation of a centralized directory of payer endpoints to 
support use of APIs developed for electronic prior authorization.  
 
Thank you for considering our recommendations, and we look forward to working with CMS to improve 
patient access to medications they need to get and stay healthy.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Amazon.com, Inc.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor / Pharmacy / Cloud services organization.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Operates Amazon Pharmacy, One Medical, AWS HealthLake, and Amazon Connect Health; describes AI, FHIR, and cloud infrastructure capabilities.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Amazon broadly supports standards-based APIs and electronic prior authorization, especially CMS alignment of medical benefit drug PA with the FHIR approach from the 2024 final rule. Amazon recommends moving toward a single FHIR-based ePA framework for both medical and pharmacy benefit drugs, rather than maintaining dual FHIR and NCPDP tracks.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS indirectly.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR sections; references CMS-0062-P and the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; Da Vinci specifications; NCPDP standards; APIs; AWS HealthLake FHIR capabilities.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: FHIR-based ePA for medical benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Aligning medical benefit drug PA with the FHIR-based approach for services will streamline implementation and data exchange between providers and payers.
- **Specific request:** Finalize FHIR-based medical benefit drug ePA requirements.

**Topic 2: Dual standards for pharmacy benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Dual-track FHIR/NCPDP standards add complexity, backend translation costs, and continued friction between systems.
- **Specific request:** Create an option to use FHIR for pharmacy benefit drug ePA, consider enforcement discretion for all-FHIR workflows, and potentially adopt NCPDP only temporarily before transitioning to FHIR-only.

**Topic 3: Decision timeframes and AI-enabled workflow acceleration**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Electronic exchange and agentic AI can help providers and payers identify information requests and streamline reviews.
- **Specific request:** Finalize reduced response times, including QHP 72-hour response requirements.

**Topic 4: API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Endpoint reporting can enable centralized payer endpoint directories needed for scalable ePA API adoption.
- **Specific request:** Finalize payer API endpoint availability reporting.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S2/S18:** Supports required FHIR-based standards and Da Vinci specifications for PA workflows, at least for medical benefit drugs.
- **S12:** Supports medical benefit drug FHIR ePA and states AWS services can support implementation.
- **S14/S22/S25:** Raises concerns about maintaining NCPDP for pharmacy benefit ePA and recommends FHIR options or transition to FHIR-only.
- **S21:** Supports reduced response times and argues electronic exchange plus AI can expedite access.
- **S23/S24/S33:** Supports API endpoint reporting and centralized endpoint directory development.
- **S44/S46/S53:** Indirectly supports broader FHIR-based standardization and phased transition away from dual/legacy approaches.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize FHIR-based ePA for medical benefit drugs.
2. Establish a clear, consistent, end-to-end FHIR-based framework for all PA workflows across medical and prescription benefits.
3. Assess an option for providers to use FHIR for pharmacy benefit drug ePA.
4. Offer enforcement discretion for organizations that use FHIR for all ePA transactions.
5. If retaining NCPDP initially, make it time-limited and transition to FHIR-only within a few years.
6. Finalize payer API endpoint reporting to support centralized directories.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Complexity from dual-track standards; backend translation between NCPDP and FHIR; continued friction and proprietary integration burden.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Added costs, burden, and failure to achieve unified data exchange.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Mapping between benefit categories and standards; pharmacy benefit standards fragmentation; need for standards community collaboration.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Amazon Pharmacy uses AI to get prescriptions into patients' hands 90% faster.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None.
- **Examples provided:** Amazon Pharmacy AI, One Medical generative AI administrative tools, Amazon Connect Health agentic AI, AWS HealthLake FHIR support.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients, providers, pharmacies, payers, technology vendors, standards developers.
- **Economic implications:** Single FHIR approach could reduce integration and translation costs; dual standards may increase costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** Amazon asserts FHIR-based infrastructure is already supportable through AWS capabilities; acknowledges pharmacy-benefit FHIR IG work is emerging.
- **Patient care impact:** Faster ePA and real-time adjudication could reduce pharmacy counter abandonment and medication access barriers.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Technical, business-oriented, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Broadly, Amazon supports provisions in the proposed rule that will leverage standards-based application programming interfaces (APIs)." - Context: Overall support.
2. "Instead of dual-track standards that add complexity, aligning on a single approach to electronic prior authorization for all medical and pharmacy benefits will reduce burden and simplify adoption." - Context: Central recommendation.
3. "CMS should establish a clear, consistent, end-to-end framework using FHIR-based APIs as the foundational standard for all prior authorization workflows." - Context: Preferred standards strategy.
4. "This information, once aggregated, will enable the creation of a centralized directory of payer endpoints." - Context: Endpoint reporting support.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Discusses FHIR implementation capabilities and AI-enabled workflows.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Evaluates FHIR versus NCPDP and recommends transition to FHIR-only.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Focuses on removing friction that prevents medication access.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for standards community collaboration on FHIR pharmacy ePA.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Directly addresses complexity from benefit-based standards split.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - AWS, Amazon Pharmacy, One Medical, and AI workflow examples show vendor perspective.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Seeks to reduce manual, duplicative, and proprietary integrations.
